appendix_1.title: Appendix 1: Proof of Theorem 1
appendix_1.heading: Appendix 1: Proof of Theorem 1
appendix_1.paragraph: Here is a restatement of Theorem 1, which will be proven in this appendix:

note.title: Theorem 1
note.heading: Theorem 1
note.paragraph: If $P$ is a regular $m \times m$ transition matrix with $m \geq 2$, then the following statements are all true.

list.item: There is a stochastic matrix Π such that limn→∞ Pn=Π.
Each column of Π is the same probability vector q.
For any initial probability vector x0, limn→∞ Pnx0=q.
The vector q is the unique probability vector that is an eigenvector of P associated with the eigenvalue 1.
All eigenvalues λ of P other than 1 have |λ|<1.

appendix_1.paragraph: The proof of Theorem 1 requires creation of an order relation for vectors, and begins with the consideration of matrices whose entries are strictly positive or nonnegative.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: An $m \times n$ matrix $A$ is positive if all its entries are positive. An $m \times n$ matrix $A$ is nonnegative if it has no negative entries.

appendix_1.paragraph: Notice that all stochastic matrices are nonnegative. The row-vector rule (Section 1.3) shows that multiplication of vectors by a positive matrix preserves order.
In addition, multiplication by nonnegative matrices “almost” preserves order in the following sense.
The first step toward proving Theorem 1 is a lemma that shows how the transpose of a stochastic matrix acts on a vector.

appendix_1.heading: Proof of Theorem 1
appendix_1.paragraph: First assume that the transition matrix $P$ is a positive stochastic matrix. As above, let $\epsilon > 0$ be the smallest entry in $P$. Consider the vector $\textbf{e}_{j}$ where $1 \leq j \leq m$. Let $M_{n}$ and $m_{n}$ be the largest and smallest entries in the vector $(P^{T})^{n}\textbf{e}_{j}$. Since $(P^{T})^{n}\textbf{e}_{j} = P^{T}(P^{T})^{n - 1}\textbf{e}_{j}$, Lemma 1 gives
Hence, by induction, it may be shown that

Since $m \geq 2$, $0 < \epsilon \leq 1/2$. Thus $0 \leq 1 - 2\epsilon < 1$, and $\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\text{lim}}\left( {M_{n} - m_{n}} \right)\, = 0$. Therefore the entries in the vector $(P^{T})^{n}\textbf{e}_{j}$ approach the same value, say $q_{j}$, as $n$ increases. Notice that since the entries in $P^{T}$ are between $0$ and $1$, the entries in $(P^{T})^{n}\textbf{e}_{j}$ must also be between $0$ and $1$, and so $q_{j}$ must also lie between $0$ and $1$. Now $(P^{T})^{n}\textbf{e}_{j}$ is the $j^{\text{t}\text{h}}$ column of $(P^{T})^{n}$, which is the $j^{\text{t}\text{h}}$ row of $P^{n}$. Therefore $P^{n}$ approaches a matrix all of whose rows are constant vectors, which is another way of saying the columns of $P^{n}$ approach the same vector $\textbf{q}$:

So Theorem 1(a) is true if $P$ is a positive matrix. Suppose now that $P$ is regular but not positive; since $P$ is regular, there is a power $P^{k}$ of $P$ that is positive. We need to show that $\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\text{lim}}\,\left( {M_{n} - m_{n}} \right)\, = 0$; the remainder of the proof follows exactly as above. No matter the value of $n$, there is always a multiple of $k$, say $rk$, with $rk < n \leq r(k + 1)$. By the proof above, $\underset{r\rightarrow\infty}{\text{lim}}\,\left( {M_{rk} - m_{rk}} \right)\, = 0$. But Equation (6) applies equally well to nonnegative matrices, so $0 \leq M_{n} - m_{n} \leq M_{rk} - m_{rk}$, and $\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\text{lim}}\,M_{n} - m_{n} = 0$, proving part (a) of Theorem 1.

To prove part (b), it suffices to show that $\textbf{q}$ is a probability vector. To see this, note that since $(P^{T})^{n}$ has row sums equal to $1$ for any $n$, $(P^{T})^{n}\textbf{u} = \textbf{u}$. Since $\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\text{lim}}\,\left( P^{T} \right)^{n} = \text{Π}^{T}$, it must be the case that $\text{Π}^{T}\textbf{u} = \textbf{u}$. Thus the rows of $\text{Π}^{T}$, and so also the columns of $\text{Π}$, must sum to $1$ and $\textbf{q}$ is a probability vector.
The proof of part (c) follows from the definition of matrix multiplication and the fact that $P^{n}$ approaches $\text{Π}$ by part (a). Let $\textbf{x}_{0}$ be any probability vector. Then
since the entries in $\textbf{x}_{0}$ sum to $1$.

To prove part (d), we calculate $P\text{Π}$. First note that $\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\text{lim}}\,P^{n + 1} = \text{Π}$. But since $P^{n + 1} = PP^{n}$, and $\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\text{lim}}\,P^{n} = \text{Π}$, $\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\text{lim}}\,P^{n + 1} = P\text{Π}$. Thus $P\text{Π} = \text{Π}$, and any column of this matrix equation gives $P\textbf{q} = \textbf{q}$. Thus $\textbf{q}$ is a probability vector that is also an eigenvector for $P$ associated with the eigenvalue $\lambda = 1$. To show that this vector is unique, let $\textbf{v}$ be any eigenvector for $P$ associated with the eigenvalue $\lambda = 1$, which is also a probability vector. Then $P\textbf{v} = \textbf{v}$, and $P^{n}\textbf{v} = \textbf{v}$ for any $n$. But by part (c), $\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\text{lim}}\,P^{n}\textbf{v} = \textbf{q}$, which can happen only if $\textbf{v} = \textbf{q}$. Thus $\textbf{q}$ is unique. Note that this part of the proof has also shown that the eigenspace associated with the eigenvalue $\lambda = 1$ has dimension $1$.

To prove part (e), let $\lambda \neq 1$ be an eigenvalue of $P$, and let $\textbf{x}$ be an associated eigenvector. Assume that $\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{m}{x_{k} \neq 0}$. Since any nonzero scalar multiple of $\textbf{x}$ will also be an eigenvector associated with $\lambda$, we may scale the eigenvector $\textbf{x}$ by the reciprocal of $\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{m}x_{k}$ to form the eigenvector $\textbf{w}$. Notice that the sum of the entries in $\textbf{w}$ is $1$. Then $P\textbf{w} = \lambda\textbf{w}$, so $P^{n}\textbf{w} = \lambda^{n}\textbf{w}$ for any $n$. By the proof of part (c), $\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\text{lim}}\,P^{n}\textbf{w} = \textbf{q}$ since the entries in $\textbf{w}$ sum to $1$. Thus
